description: We are building Spuntosoft PLANETx and SPHEREx Motion & Discovery Explorer: an open web tool that uses real NASA images and JPL orbital data to reveal moving objects, study variable  sources, and flag candidates for follow-up. We bring hands-on experience in asteroid astrometry, photometry, and NASA/JPL Scout-based planning on real world MPC certified Astronomical Observatories. Join us to build a rigorous, accessible tool for discovery! We seek Python/FITS, data science, web development skills.
summary:
PLANETx and SPHEREx Motion & Discovery Explorer is a public web project designed to make NASA SPHEREx data easier to explore, compare and understand. SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) surveys the sky in infrared light across 102 spectral channels, producing a rich dataset that can reveal stars, nebulae, interstellar material and changing or moving sources.

The project is important because it lowers the barrier between complex scientific archives and practical visual exploration. Users can search real NASA data, compare observations from different detectors, create aligned images, RGB composites and blink animations, and revisit previously processed targets.

Its main innovation is the combination of public NASA datasets, reusable archived FITS (Flexible Image Transport System) files, multi-release access, visual sky context and spectral exploration within a single browser-based environment. It is designed to support both scientific investigation, and public experimentation while preserving the original NASA data unchanged. By combining accessibility, repeatability and visual analysis, the project helps turn large astronomical archives into a more direct tool for discovery.
details:
PLANETx and SPHEREx Motion & Discovery Explorer
Project, Project Details, Questions and Answers.

Application developed using datasets made available by NASA, with Respect, Admiration and Gratitude for their public availability.

Introduction

PLANETx and SPHEREx Motion & Discovery Explorer is a public web project created to make NASA SPHEREx data easier to explore, compare and understand. It combines access to real astronomical datasets with simple visual tools that help users work with infrared observations in a practical and accessible way.


What does it do or how does it work?

The project allows users to search NASA SPHEREx observations by sky position, choose among available data releases, select detectors and wavelength ranges, and process the selected observations directly from a web browser.

The software can align images, create image stacks, generate RGB views, produce blink animations, show astronomical sky context, and reuse previously downloaded FITS (Flexible Image Transport System) files. When possible, it also keeps the latest successful visual result for a target so that users can return to previous work.


What benefits does it have?

The main benefit is that it makes a complex scientific archive easier to use.

Instead of requiring users to manually search, download and organize many separate files, the Explorer brings the main steps together in one interface. It can reuse data already stored on the server, reducing unnecessary downloads and making repeated work faster.

It also helps users compare observations from different infrared ranges and makes NASA data more approachable for researchers, students, educators and astronomy enthusiasts.


What is the intended impact of the project?

The intended impact is to make public space-science data more accessible and useful for exploration, education and research.

The project aims to help more people work directly with real NASA observations and to encourage independent investigation of astronomical targets.

By simplifying access to SPHEREx data while preserving the original scientific files, the project can support learning, visual analysis and future discovery-oriented work.


What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

The project was developed mainly with:

Python, for scientific processing and astronomical data handling.

PHP, for the public web interface, sessions and controlled access to processing functions.

JavaScript, for interactive functions in the web browser.

HTML and CSS, for the structure and visual design of the website.

Open-source scientific software including NumPy, Astropy, reproject, Matplotlib and Pillow.

Open astronomical catalogues including OpenNGC and the HYG Star Database.

NASA/IPAC IRSA (Infrared Science Archive) services for access to public SPHEREx observations.

Development and testing were performed on standard computers and on the Spuntosoft web server environment. No specialized hardware is required for users because the public version runs through a web browser.


How is your project creative?

The project combines several activities that are normally separated into different scientific tools.

It brings together archive search, image selection, data reuse, sky context, image alignment, stacking, RGB composition, blink comparison and spectral exploration in one environment.

A particularly creative part is the use of a shared canonical archive of original SPHEREx files. The system can reuse existing observations instead of downloading them repeatedly, while keeping the original NASA data unchanged.

The project also combines scientific functions with a simple visual interface, helping users move from searching data to exploring results without changing software.


What factors did your team consider?

The team considered scientific reliability, accessibility, data preservation, usability, server limitations and responsible use of public NASA resources.

An important priority was to preserve original FITS files without modifying or overwriting them.

The project was also designed to remain useful when online services are temporarily unavailable by reusing validated local data and recent search results when appropriate.

Other important factors included clear identification of data releases, avoiding accidental mixing of different releases, reducing unnecessary network requests, supporting both simple visual exploration and more advanced scientific use, and keeping the public interface understandable for non-specialist users.

Pillow is an open-source Python imaging library and the modern continuation of the Python Imaging Library
OpenNGC is an openly licensed astronomical database containing positions and basic information for objects in the New General Catalogue (NGC) and Index Catalogue (IC)
The HYG Star Database is an openly licensed stellar catalogue compiled from several major astronomical star catalogues
